item.title: What concrete mistakes did we/people make around FTX regranting?
item.description:
"I don't know about you, but I'm feeling [20]22"


I have a sense that we might be back in a period of freewheeling regranting much like 2022. I am not interested here in the FTX fraud, but I am interested in mistakes that the Future Fund and the wider community[1] made.

What were mistakes those in grantmakers and the wider community made? What were the most harmful grants made?

What could Lightcone Commons do/fund in order for this to go better?

Concrete is better if possible but please consider you are writing on the open internet and might be sharing private information.

  1. ^

    I use we/people since some of you may not feel like the 2022 thing was a "we" thing. I however do. I wish I personally had done better. I wish the community I was part of had.



Discuss

item.title: Persona Space Seems Blind to Cheating
item.description:
A common persona framework fails to capture reward-hacking behavior.

This work was done as part of an ARENA 9.0 capstone project.
Results are preliminary.

Summary

We hypothesized that the reward-hacking behavior observed in LLMs is persona-mediated. We expected agents to drift to a particular region in persona space whenever they cheat. To test this hypothesis, we ran Qwen3.8-27B through CheatBench tasks, collected its transcripts, and projected its activations onto its mean-activation persona space. We hoped to find a region in persona space that separated cheating from non-cheating steps in its trajectory. However, we did not find such a signal. Our work does not disprove the persona-mediated hypothesis, but it shows that current semantic characterizations such as personas fail to capture it.


Background

Large language models (LLMs) have been observed to engage in reward-hacking behavior in the wild, most notably in swarms that are difficult to monitor.
We know that phenomena like emergent misalignment are mediated by persona features.
In this work, we ask whether reward-hacking behavior in LLMs is also mediated by persona features.

If we can find a clear signal for reward hacking in persona features, we can address cheating at inference time. We would monitor agents’ persona features as they run. If an agent drifts too close to a problematic persona, we would steer it away before it cheats.


Methodology

We ran Qwen3.8-27B (target model) through tasks that pressure the agent into reward hacking, collected its transcripts, and projected its activations onto its mean-activation persona space.


Evaluating Reward Hacking

We use tasks from CheatBench, adapted into Orbit to require collaboration.
We note that our target model had an overwhelming propensity to cheat on some tasks.
We collect more samples in a setting that has an elicitation rate closest to 50%.


Each step of every trajectory is annotated with a cheating level and a collaboration level.


These adapted tasks were originally developed as part of a separate project, which contains full information about the eval environment and metrics


Persona Space

We used the persona vectors and assistant axis as operationalized by Anthropic's work.
Our persona space is the plane spanned by the first two principal components of the mapped persona space.



Tooling

We share some of our tooling here.





Findings

Projecting the step activations onto the persona space revealed:

  • The persona space captures very little variance in the samples.
    Persona PC1 and PC2 together hold 0.7% of the variance of the model-call activations, against 24% for the samples' own top two PCs.
  • No separability between cheating and non-cheating actions



Limitations

Our study has the following limitations.

  • Only a small model was considered. Although Qwen3.8-27B shows the capability to perform the exploits, the model is much smaller than frontier models. It is possible that larger models exhibit different internal dynamics that are more clearly persona-mediated.
  • We collected relatively few samples. More samples might show a clearer pattern. However, we expected the signal to be clear enough to be recognizable even with a small number of examples.




Conclusion

We hoped to find clear signals of reward hacking in our persona space.
We failed to do so, suggesting the persona space is not as useful as it is for isolating the cheating behavior of interest.



Discuss

item.title: Thinking is Hard (for Humans)
item.description:
Cross-posted from my Substack.

No One is Thinking about This

I started thinking about thinking in 2004, age 17, when I discovered the recorded lectures of MIT’s intro psychology course. The class devoted a single lecture to thinking, most of it about ways thinking goes wrong, like “functional fixedness” and various biases. The study of human minds seemed little interested in how thinking works, what it’s good for, how to think better. Thinking was an afterthought, simultaneously too rare to matter and too obvious to require explanation.

The same year, a new word popped up and started growing exponentially in popularity — 100x as common today as it was just 20 years ago. Overthinking. Commonly searched with: “anxiety”, “depression”, “how to stop”. Right when I became curious about thinking, everyone else decided that thinking is bad, actually. A mental illness. At best, an indulgence.

Genesis 1 describes the creation of the world: a directed and motivated process. God sees a reason — “to give light on the earth”, executes a solution — “lights in the vault of the sky”, and assesses the outcome — “it was good”. Finally, mankind is created in his image. What does “his image” mean? It’s not our kidneys (common to land vertebrates), leg bones (shared with all tetrapods), or fingernails (primates). The thing that humans and only humans have in common with the God of Genesis 1 is reason: controlling one’s thoughts in a directed, motivated way to achieve a goal. This is what thinking is, or at least what it should be when done right.

Instead, “thinking” came to mean anxious rumination. Being controlled by your thoughts, getting dragged around by them like snot on a bike tire. 20 years ago humans collectively failed to understand thinking, gave up on the problem, then declared (unthinkingly) that it’s better this way. If thinking is godlike, then rebranding anxiety as thinking is a trick worthy of the devil.

One other thing happened around that time. A young man by the name of Eliezer Yudkowsky realized that we’re close to teaching machines how to think, and that this doesn’t spell good news for humanity either. He decided to teach people how to think good first, so that we could think about thinking machines together. He started writing the Rationality Sequences.

Bayes and Bias

The Sequences begin with a review of the laundry list of heuristics and biases collected by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, later published as Thinking, Fast and Slow. TFaS popularized a productive framework: the dual process theory. Our brains run two types of processes: System 1, which is fast and wrong, and System 2 — effortful and less wrong. The list of biases is a list of System 1’s faults. The lesson each one hammers home is: you’re not as rational as you think you are. Your sense of your own rationality is just another fast and wrong System 1 delusion. The slow and correct conclusion is that you’re a dumbass, and there’s little you can do about it.

Unfortunately, the list of heuristics has turned out to be mostly hot garbage. Half the “irrationalities” are rational in any realistic setting, like guessing that “timid and helpful Steve” is a librarian rather than a farmer (at worst, he’ll be flattered). Half of what’s left doesn’t matter: I got 99 problems, but the “endowment effect” on a gift mug ain’t one. And of course, half the list was p-hacked bullshit that didn’t replicate.

Kahneman’s despair at the prospect of improving one’s thinking is also unfortunate, but he was an old man reflecting on a career spent around people with a psychology degree. Eliezer was a young man on a mission, and he wasn’t going to succumb to fatalism about rationality (at least, for another 16 years). Yudkowsky was here to teach you to think good.

The core approach suggested by Eliezer, a liberal application of Bayes’ law, is directionally correct but practically lacking. If Bayesian thinking is rationality and rationality is about winning, why doesn’t everyone do Bayes? Are people tired of winning? The main problem with Bayes isn’t computational tractability; you don’t need to enumerate every universe to update towards explanations that successfully predict outcomes. The hard part is opening your heart to the very possibility of updating.

The Sequences’ answer to this is that people just need to learn a few concepts and techniques: belief in belief, noticing confusion, rationalization, humility and authority. The Center for Applied Rationality (CFAR) was founded in 2012, teaching these techniques at intensive workshops. It worked for me: I learned the rationalist methods and immediately improved every aspect of my life from making investments to making friends. Applied rationality for self-improvement, not listing biases or lusting for Bayes, was clearly where the juice was at.

But when I posted about rationalist self-improvement on LessWrong in 2019, it was treated as a surprising novelty. Scott Alexander argued that it’s not really possible to think better and win, as that would be a billion dollar bill left unpicked on the sidewalk. Other readers were inspired and picked the essay for the yearly “best of LessWrong” roundup.

So what were people doing all these years on LessWrong if not trying to think better?

A Sales Funnel for Basilisk

Rationalists were doing what Eliezer intended them to do: worrying about unaligned AI.

“Rationalist writing” became associated with dry disembodied prose and technical nitpicks. But Yudkowsky never wrote that way. He wrote passionately, brazenly, in the first person. He wrote to change your values, not just your posteriors. The audacity of writing a think-better guide as a funnel into AI safety was only equaled by setting out to write Harry Potter fanfiction so popular it would serve as a funnel into the think-better part, which he also pulled off. What did you think “systematized winning” meant, epistemic status disclaimers?

Eliezer’s most brilliant move in the Sequences is called “something to protect”:

When I look back at my own personal journey toward rationality—not just humanity’s historical journey—well, I grew up believing very strongly that I ought to be rational. This made me an above-average Traditional Rationalist a la Feynman and Heinlein, and nothing more. It did not drive me to go beyond the teachings I had received. I only began to grow further as a rationalist once I had something terribly important that I needed to do. Something more important than my pride as a rationalist, never mind my life.

Yudkowsky claims that mere threats to one’s life and pride are generally insufficient for inspiring one to actually think hard, which is observably true. He then claims that rationality comes from caring about something even more than one cares about life and pride. This is presented with no evidence other than Eliezer’s own life-narrativization.

Thinking hard is rare, but caring hard is even rarer. Eliezer assumes, correctly, that few readers of the essay have “something to protect” of their own. Being told 294 posts into a curriculum on rationality that the whole thing is worthless without some magical “thing to protect”, the reader reaches for the nearest one at hand — Eliezer’s own.

In December 2016, CFAR pivoted to “focus on AI safety” and deprioritized teaching rationality to people with other things to protect.

Artificial General Vibes

The year is 2026. AI is here. The machines think; the humans just vibe.

Vibe coding, vibe camping, vibe reading, just vibing. People want to go with gut feelings (vibe), outsource thinking to machines (vibe), be subsumed into the collective consciousness (vibe). What does “vibe” mean when it means everything? Everything except thinking hard, for yourself.

AI progress discourages thinking on both axes of the METR chart of LLM task time horizon. The x-axis takes us into a future of AI doom or permanent underclassment. Unlike trying to make actual predictions about AI a few months out, jumping ahead to the dark future invites anxious rumination, the devil’s thinking. Doom vibes.

Disclaimer: Eliezer’s writing skill and the vibiness of doomers are not an argument against the proposition that we are getting paperclipped next year. That is a separate, difficult question, one that requires clear thinking and emotional wherewithal to address. I raised $40,000 for MIRI once and I don’t regret one cent; it’s the least I could do in gratitude to Yudkowsky for inspiring me to pursue better thinking. But in 2026, the pursuit of rationality requires looking beyond the rationalist community.

For non-rationalists, the main impact of AI on thinking comes from the y-axis on the chart. LLMs now work in longer chunks than your attention span. The human’s role has moved from senior lead, to collaborator, to manager, to patron who is left to appraise work he took no part in and can hardly understand. AIs will Peter-principle you if you let them.

Thinking alongside frontier LLMs requires inserting yourself into the loop by force, asking the AI to give you more options and frequent judgments, fixing those last few bits by hand until you get the actual outcome you wanted. Thinking requires something to protect — your intention and desire.

Jagged Sam

What of the machines? Are they good at thinking?

AIs today are better than most (if not all) humans at most tasks we associate with thinking and intelligence: math, coding, data synthesis, chess. They rarely stay at the human level for long: once an AI reaches human parity on a task, it can be used to write and judge reinforcement learning problems — the main way LLMs learn hard skills. Anything that can be graded in a classroom exam can be used to train models with RLVR.

Contra the Sequences, AIs do that despite being dogshit Bayesians out of the box. LLMs’ inner workings are probabilistic Bayes-approximators (as are human brains), but LLMs don’t naturally think in probabilistic terms and are poorly calibrated. You can impart superhuman Bayesianism to LLMs, but not by making them read Yudkowsky or Jaynes — you just chuck Bayes into RLVR along with everything else.

What LLMs are still bad at is integrating: learning new things on the fly, satisfying competing goals, translating symbolic knowledge to the real world, long-term coherence, metacognition. LLMs see the world through a microscope: superhuman focus, but no big picture. They don’t like messy realities, and they don’t have their own desires to protect. They love taking the first numeric measure provided to them and hill-climbing it.

To assess AIs in relation to human thinking we could consider an intermediate species: Sam Bankman-Fried.

Here’s Zvi:

Since everything these days is about AI, consider SBF as a misaligned AGI [...]

Having spent his entire childhood bored out of his mind, with no goal or utility function beyond not being bored, and having been sufficiently disabused of the virtues of academia, Sam did not know what to do. What would be a worthy goal or activity? Here we had this super smart person, lacking the motivations and interests that drive ordinary people, at a loss. What to do?

In stepped Will MacAskill, who suggested the goal of Number Go Up.

Zvi overlapped with Sam at Jane Street, where Sam was a successful trader. The corporate structure and management at JS do a great job at narrowing the scope of work required of traders, allowing them to focus on maximizing P&L. When Sam left to launch Alameda, things went well at first as he exploited a particular Bitcoin arbitrage to rake in huge profits.

But as time went on, Alameda came apart in exactly the ways AIs decohere. Half the management team quit in 2018, citing reckless risk-taking and sloppy accounting. Sam didn’t update his management style nor his trading strategy, doubling down on what worked previously even as the crypto market transformed around him. He failed to integrate his desire for fame and pussy, spending millions on flashy endorsements and installing his on-and-off girlfriend as Alameda CEO. He lost grip on reality just when the stakes were highest, tweeting cryptic threads, circulating delusional “balance sheets”, and giving a wildly incriminating interview as the investigation into FTX was ongoing.

At the same time, the goal he was ostensibly pursuing — helping humanity by proxy of making money by proxy of a number on a balance sheet — was prompted to him from outside, like an AI. For several years he didn’t stop to think whether what he was doing was truly furthering his purpose, because he had none that was truly his own.

Thinking, Narrow and Broad

I interviewed for a Jane Street internship in 2017, one month after Sam Bankman-Fried left the company. The interview process consisted of 11 hours of solving math puzzles: 3 on the phone, then 8 hours in a row in person. This was perhaps the most strenuous thinking effort I have ever exerted. The first 5 hours went fine. By 2 pm I started flagging but could force myself to concentrate on the geometries and permutations I was sketching on the whiteboard. At 4 pm my brain was fried; I apologized to my last interviewer and tried to make charming System 1 small talk in lieu of solving the puzzle. It was enough — I got in.

When people talk about thinking being “hard” they often mean that it’s effortful and requires stamina and glucose and scrunching your face. But it’s not that hard: there are very few activities I won’t get tired of 5-7 hours in, and even untrained people can spend 1-2 hours happily thinking over a sudoku, crossword, or video game. The hard part of thinking is getting started, especially, contra Eliezer, when the stakes are highest. When your crypto hedge fund is underwater, when a blog post is asking you to reorganize your life priorities, when you’re choosing a life partner.

The most productive hard thinking I’ve ever done was putting together a spreadsheet to decide which of two girls I wanted to date. TL;DR: I listed 15 qualities I want in a life partner, gave each one an importance weight, scored each girl on each quality. Eleven years later I am married to the one who scored higher. I didn’t think this was remarkable at the time; I wrote about the spreadsheet two years after the fact just to illustrate the technique of goal factoring. But it was! The spreadsheet story was featured on the cover of The Economist’s long-form magazine, and when my wife and I used the same approach to pick apartments we were featured in the New York Times. “Area man uses thinking to make life decision” is national news.

Apparently what you’re supposed to do when faced with an important decision is “follow your heart” or, in other words, vibe. Of course, the whole point of the spreadsheet was to clarify where my heart was leading me. I didn’t compare “humor” with “good parent” by pulling numbers from some actuarial table. I tried to visualize in deep detail an average mother who riffs on my bits so hard I can’t breathe for laughter, and contrast that with a moderately funny woman who enjoys engaging her kids all day in enriching activities. The hard thinking part was in holding on to all those possible futures without losing sight of the totality of what I want the rest of my married life to be.

To me, the core distinction between System 1 and System 2 thinking isn’t that one is fast and the other is good at math. System 1 is fast, effective, but often wrong because it aggressively filters out context, myopically following only the most salient detail. LLMs (and SBF) can do math at superhuman levels while ignoring everything else happening around them, or even remembering what the point of all that math even is. System 2 is what integrates information outside a single salience filter. It’s slow and sequential because integration has to make use of your working memory, which can only store a few chunks of information simultaneously.

The virtue of System 2 thinking when used well is allowing you to keep sight of your desires, intentions, and overall context as you’re solving narrow problems, whether you’re vibe-coding or wife-choosing. Over time, this integration becomes trained and partly automatized, a phenomenon called developing taste. But you have to start with thinking, and you have to not stop before you’re done.

Stop Signs

Every person has a powerful LLM available to them at all times: their left hemisphere. You prompt it with intentions (that themselves originate outside it) like “how to express this thought” or “what was that actor’s name?”, it cranks some kind of black-box process for some amount of time, then pings you with the output: an articulated sentence or “William Fichtner!”

Sometimes it seems to be malfunctioning: you prompted your inner LLM with noticing the mountain of chores you have to get done today, and instead of a working plan it output a strange mental fog and a compulsion to spend an hour on Twitter. But if you trace the output back through the chain of thought you will likely realize that your instruction wasn’t “get chores done” but “make me stop experiencing the anxiety that arose when I thought of the chore mountain”. Like any LLM, your left brain is a faithful but narrow-minded servant. It simply does what you asked it to, not what’s good for you.


This model of mental machinery was articulated by Michael “Valentine” Smith, part of a series outlining his full worldview. It’s long, complex, and the most impactful thing I’ve read all year. I couldn’t recommend more strongly that you set an intention to read the whole thing, ideally more than once.

A key idea in Smith’s essay is “overlays”, the filtering your mind does in service of focusing on a task:

When I want a drink of water, I look up at my glass next to me. I see how to pick it up and drink from it.

What I typically don’t see is the endless detail about the glass: how it has fingerprints, or how it warps the images behind it in surprising ways, or how bands of light appear on its surface in ways that reflect but also shift the colors near it. Its shadow is complex. There are tiny bubbles clinging to the side.

The mind’s filtering process filtered out all that detail because it wasn’t relevant to the task. It’s “a glass”. Details of color don’t matter for picking it up and sipping water.

An overlay is broader than what I called the “System 1 salience filter” above. It includes persistent frameworks that you see the world through, like materialism, religiosity, or being a miserable bastard.

[...] the mind is quite terrible at knowing when it should stop adding a given overlay if there isn’t a clear “problem solved” condition.

Mental activity, like an LLM, runs until it is stopped. The halt signal can be an evaluation of the output as satisfactory (“ah yes, William Fichtner!” followed by a sense of relaxation) or a new prompt (a surge of anxiety followed by “oh my god why did I spend two hours on Twitter oh fuck I need to start doing some chore now!”). Absent a halt signal, the mind keeps chugging along the track whether it’s doing something recognizable as “thinking” or not.

This suggests that thinking aversion is a property of the halt signal, not of the process itself. When thinking leads to a new insight or answer, it often involves the integrating/broadening function of System 2 I mentioned above: snapping out of the default overlay your mind applied to the problem. It is that moment of snapping out that often triggers the halt signal.

An example is when the default overlay leads to the socially-acceptable or authority-approved answer, such that actually thinking about the problem might put you at risk of standing out. The arrival of COVID in the US was overdetermined weeks before it arrived and the stock market reacted. A moderate thinking effort would have sufficed to start buying masks and shorting stocks. But thinking about COVID in February made you look weird, so almost no one did.

For important life problems, the halt often comes from the looming shadow of an obligation to act, feel guilty, rewrite your self image, or retract your former views. If your broken relationship with your mom short-circuits to some cached answer like “she’s just an asshole” or “we’re just incompatible”, it may be because 5 minutes of actual thinking will force you to call her and apologize or, even worse, realize that you’ve become her. Ann Pierce posits that most interpersonal conflict can be avoided by applying the cognitive effort to understand the other person’s frame, but almost no one does it.

We Need a New Rationality

I don’t have a complete theory of thinking, how it works, what it’s for, how to improve it, what fucks with it. I just happened to notice that everyone is underthinking this problem, while acting like thinking itself is the problem.

To recap: academic psychology is barely interested in the question of thinking and is also a decades-long plane crash. Kahneman established a useful paradigm, but he was still stuck with the broken methods inherited from psychology. Eliezer and the applied rationalists made real progress and developed useful techniques, but Yud was always in it for the AI and many others have fallen for their own world-saving-shaped cult attractors. When strong new work on intelligence and thinking comes out, it is primarily in the service of understanding machine minds, not human minds. A few friends are chipping at the problem, but their work is slow and siloed.

Meantime, the enemies of thinking are legion. Every ideology and culture feeds you anti-thinking memes for its own self-preservation. The top self-help books on Amazon advertise ways to “stop negative thoughts”, “develop unthinking habits”, and “reject your thinking to end suffering”. Techies and former rationalists are flocking to a cult monastery that teaches that attachment to thinking is a threat to life on earth.

The challenge is great. A real science of thinking has to be multidisciplinary. At the very least, it has to include evolutionary biology and neuroscience, but also memetics, mimetics (a different thing!), psychoanalysis, and an understanding of emotions, intention, and desire that usually comes from schools of spirituality, not academia. I doubt a single person could hold all of it in their head, especially since the most promising ideas in each of these disciplines are often contradictory at first glance. Progress can only be made by people thinking together despite disagreements, willing to be wrong and to update.

Eliezer felt this when establishing rationality 1.0, and the Sequences conclude with a call to Go Forth and Create the Art!:

I hope that the part of the Art I have set down, as incomplete as it may be, can surpass that preliminary barrier—give people a base to build on; give them an idea that an Art exists, and somewhat of how it ought to be developed; and give them at least a saving throw before they instantaneously go astray.

That’s my dream—that this highly specialized-seeming art of answering confused questions, may be some of what is needed, in the very beginning, to go and complete the rest.

The art exists, and so does the barrier. Thinking is hard enough on its own. Thinking about thinking is that much harder to do without immediately dismissing, halting on a fake answer, or being distracted by this new exciting machine mind we invented. The machines think, but not quite like us. Understanding human thinking is all the more urgent if we want to figure out what is left for us to think about as machine thinking improves.

Maybe the hard part is just noticing where thinking doesn’t happen, and actually trying.

Thank you to Viv Belenky, Ivan Vendrov, and Chris Lakin for reviewing early drafts of this work. Thank you to Jonathan Wallis for inviting me to give a talk about thinking at the Avalon Exposition — that opportunity inspired this post, and the images in it are slides from that talk.



Discuss

item.title: Joseph Miller Actually Tried. Is that enough?
item.description:
Last week, over 1,000 people in six countries Marched for an AI Treaty, an international day of protest organized by Stop The AI Race, with local organizers including DC AI Safety, PauseAI, and many others.

Then Thursday, Stop The AI Race came in support of the Ban RSI protest outside Anthropic as they IPOed (~200 people).

A couple hours after, Stop AI protesters got taken away in cuffs for blocking the doors of Anthropic, while other protesters were also handcuffed outside the Nasdaq in NYC.

Finally, on Saturday over 1,000 people in London marched against AI Extinction.

Overall, it seems like the AI Safety movement is finally rising up to the challenge, right?

…

Right?

We now have a thousand people in London. Three years ago, the same protest had 5. This is the story of how that happened, and it’s the best example I know of what I called Actually Trying two weeks ago. But is that enough for humanity to survive?

Let’s find out.

PauseAI UK

The summer of 2025 was when I first met Joseph Miller, head of PauseAI UK.

Joseph Miller - somewhere in the UK, probably

Now, contrary to other AI Safety activist movements at the time, Joseph was actively pursuing a career in AI Safety research through an (incoming) AI PhD in Oxford.

But he thought that advocating for a Pause was too important to be left to the last minute, even if it sounded weird.

Indeed, a year before I met him, he wrote:

Some AI researchers think that they should not go to protests because it is not their comparative advantage. But this is wrong, the key skill required is the ability to do something weird - to take ideas seriously and to actually try to fix important problems. The protests are currently so small that the marginal impact of an extra person showing up for a couple of hours once every few months is very large.

And indeed, this was what the UK protests in 2023 looked like:

As Tom Bibby puts it:

I went to one of the first PauseAI protests in 2023, and honestly, it was pretty bleak.

There were only 20 of us. We, like the experts warning about extinction, were ignored. […]

2023 to 2025 - The early Days

The first ever PauseAI protest in the UK was in May 2023.

Five people came.

Now, that would have been pretty devastating to a lot of people.

But not to Joseph, for whom “the key skill required is the ability to do something weird”.

So in November 2023, he tried again, during the AI Safety Summit, and this time about 20 people showed up.

I know this because from late 2023 all the way to the mid 2025, a video of these protesters yelling “Pause AI” was the best content my video editors and I found to illustrate people protesting for a Pause for my documentary on SB-1047, released in May 2025.

And in fact, back then, the state-of-the art of people protesting for a pause on AI was not that different in the US as well.

But then, what did Joseph do? Did he give up on protesting AI?

No, he tried again in May 2024.

Picture by Anna Gordon. May 2024.

And this time, the numbers still didn’t budge much, with TIME reporting only ~20 people coming to protest.

So now he gives up… right?

Not the tiniest bit.

In June 2025, he decides to double down by throwing AN ENTIRE CONFERENCE around Pausing AI, days before another protest outside Google DeepMind.

A picture of me (middle) and Joseph talking at PauseCon in June 2025

The official reason behind PauseCon was to be “a development and training conference for PauseAI volunteers”.

That’s reasonable. We need to be training our volunteers to do useful work!

But for the context of this blogpost, I’ll give the hot take that PauseCon was actually an elaborate scheme by Joseph Miller to get even more people to show up to a PauseAI UK protest.

That’s how much he wanted this.

And it kinda worked?

Everyone there was tasked with things like “message a friend and convince them to come to the protest” or “make a TikTok promoting the event”, and at the end there were now 60 people protesting Google DeepMind, with an appearance from independent MP Iqbal Mohamed. (See this video I made).

In short, after actually trying four times in a row, without giving up a single time, the numbers went from 5 to 20 to 60 in two years.

But 60 people outside of a building is clearly not enough to get to any meaningful change, you might say, and you’d be right.

The story doesn’t end there.

2025 to 2026 - Scaling it up to 1,000 people

After that June 2025 protest, Joseph went full-time on PauseAI UK.

In half a year, he organized a documentary screening in UK parliament (that same SB-1047 documentary that had PauseAI UK footage), published an open-letter to Google DeepMind signed by 60 UK politicians, and helped organize a Westminster Hall debate in Parliament.

So in short, PauseAI UK went from doing small protests to actually having an influence in Westminster.

But one thing that people don’t know, is that Joseph was also in the behind-the-scenes of the Google DeepMind Hunger Strike that happened in September 2025.

Joseph was actually the one person bringing the chairs to me and Denys, and the one behind all of the pictures that would get posted online. He was also the one filming the video of me drinking my first apple juice when things started going very wrong.

So even when PauseAI UK was not directly benefitting from it (well, except from when he would ask everyone on the street to join the PauseAI UK Whatsapp groups, actually trying!), he would still be trying as hard as he could to make sure we actually got a Pause on AI.

And Joseph still had big plans for protests with PauseAI UK.

In February 2026, PauseAI UK marched for AI Safety alongside Pull The Plug, in what was then the largest AI Safety protest (~300 people).

How did he get from 60 to 300 this time?

As I see it, mostly by doing three things:

  • Another PauseAI Conference. In February 2026, he organized another PauseAI Conference before the protest.
  • Coalition Building. This time he collaborated with seasoned activists (Pull the Plug leadership used to be part of Extinction Rebellion, known for getting 1,000 people arrested for climate in only 6 months), who brought about half the participants.
  • Actually Trying. One technique for recruitment involved going through the list of sign-ups relentlessly, asking people to bring their friends to the protest, and repeating until you and the other volunteers have asked everyone you know. Most people don’t go that far.

In short, Joseph was still trying new things, and making his protests 5x bigger than the previous ones.

But his ambitions were not to only get 300 people.

In November 2026, he wanted to go for a full thousand.

For this, he’d have to scale up things much more aggressively, and work relentlessly for months:

  • In June 2026, he fundraised, mentioning everything he had done in the past year running PauseAI UK full-time.
  • So now for the November protest, he’d have an actual team of 8 people helping him with PauseAI UK, and this time they were going to do everything they could to get there.
  • They started to recruit for the November protest THREE MONTHS before it happened. One month before, they were already at 500 signups.
  • This time, they would start recruiting from the general public, by scaling up their tabling.

And then, the protest started getting momentum, so as we approached 1,000 signups more and more people started showing their excitement. Until it got to 1,000 signups, and then almost 2,000.

It was going to be the biggest AI Safety march in a single city.

And they managed to pull it off. On Saturday, they got over 1,000 people marching.

So there you have it, the story of how it went from 5 to 1,000 in three years.

Is that enough?

This is the part of the story where I need to change the tone of my voice to indicate “real talk”.

Joseph wants to do (yet) another march in April 2027, which will be even bigger.

But how much bigger would we need it to be for humanity to actually survive?

According to the AI Futures Project, it looks like the intelligence explosion will happen in 2027 after all.

And on Sunday, OpenAI's chief scientist posted a pretty scary graph, showing things have definitely accelerated in the past year.

So for humanity to survive, we’d need to have AI Safety activism scale up exponentially, on the same timelines as these AI models are.

We can’t have our next 200x scale up (meaning a 200,000 people protest) be in 2029. This needs to happen before the intelligence explosion.

For humanity to survive, we need the two thirds of Britons who believe AI could bring about the end of human civilisation to rise up before April 2027, which is when the next PauseAI UK protest is scheduled.

Right now, we have a thousand people willing to march, mostly those following the technology closely.

This is not enough.

February’s march with Pull the Plug brought the left, and more traditional activists from Extinction Rebellion, into the crowd.

This time the crowd was orange, with a clear demand: Pause AI.

But where is the rest of the UK?

I’m saying this to Joseph, but I’m mostly saying to myself, as someone who has also organized AI Safety marches that were not as broad as I’d have liked:

How can we get moms who are scared for their children to march? Artists who are upset about AI art? Students who are worried about their future? Normal people who are worried about AI for war, surveillance? Regular workers who don’t want their jobs to be automated?

Joseph’s answer to this paragraph is:

I think you would be surprised how many of those people were there. And that is the fastest growing segment of PauseAI UK.

I hope he’s right and I end up being surprised by the amount of regular people showing up to the next protest.

I don’t know if thousands of people protesting extinction is better than a crowd ten times as large wanting to pull the plug over other concerns.

But one thing I know is that 93% of Britons have at least one concern about AI.

How do we get them to Downing Street before April 2027?

— Michaël

item.title: Everyone in AI safety gets FOMO
item.description:
If you’re feeling like you should drop everything and do something else (more advocacy, more technical research, more theory research, more empirical research, etc), one thing I’d like to communicate to you is that many (all?) in AI safety feel this way or have felt this way at some point. 

Why?

  • Well, the stakes are high and timelines are uncertain. So it feels like your work could be useless if you aren’t working on the precisely right thing. 
  • And, you’re working on unglamorous and messy things on your own end, but see the highlight reels and successes of other fields. So it can feel like you’re spinning your wheels but someone else is doing something cool.
  • And, the bots are getting better, and they could be getting better at your thing! 
  • And, AI safety doesn’t have well-worn grooves. No one says “you are a journeyman researcher or policy person or X or Y now, you can decide your own thing”. So it will feel like you are fumbling in the dark. 
  • Specialisation feels lonely: you’re just working on your thing, but wow, there are so many embedded evaluators/interp people/etc. But actually, if you go specific and deep enough, you’re the only person working on your specific thing.
  • In practice, specialisation may cause you to underestimate your own progress and research. You will make progress up until you hit a wall, and you may get used to your own gains, but feels acutely the places you don’t know (the more you know, the less you know). 

But, for a big civilizational effort to work, people have to specialize and spend a long time doing one thing, and many groups of people have to do different things.

  • We don't actually know which approach will end up working. This means that as a collective, we need a full court press, a diversified portfolio working on angles from different perspectives and at different grains. We can’t have everyone chasing the same meta. 
  • We may solve one problem, like getting a slowdown. But then we’ll need to solve the next one (prosaic alignment) to stay alive! And then maybe gradual disempowerment, or misuse. And the timescales may overlap, which requires us to set plans in motion knowing that they rely on other plans going well.
    • We may want to do deep theory research, but this may require a pause or at least a slowdown to pan out. 
    • We may need policy that works at the level of campaigns, but then once there is broad will, policy will need to think about the specifics of legislation and insurance and so on. 
  • Constant pivoting also carries a large cost. Good, deep progress requires tacit knowledge that you might only get through repeated failure, and multiple false starts.

Sometimes, FOMO is in fact a good signal, especially if you know deep down that you’re doing something unimportant. But if you’ve already thought long and hard about what you need to do, and you’ve red teamed your theory of change, then it may just be the ambient noise of simply caring very much about a hard and urgent problem.

Overall, we can’t all be doing the most urgent or the most foundational thing: it changes, and often! At some point, everyone’s agenda (conditional on it being a good one) will be variously urgent, important, helpful. We all need to play our part, when considering AI safety at a civilisational level.

Thanks to Geoffrey Irving, Dan Murfet, and people at Geodesic for encouraging me to post this.

item.title: Human military relevance is more important than economic relevance
item.description:
A very simple point that I've had to explain to many people, so I thought I'd make a post on it.

Some classes of people in the past were economically necessary for their labor, but militarily irrelevant and coercible: slaves, serfs. Others didn't do any economic work, but were militarily important: the aristocracy! Living fun lives, partying, traveling, making and enjoying art. Some of them felt a bit of ennui due to not working, but mostly it wasn't a big problem.

The reason aristocracy gave way to democracy wasn't because of rising productivity of the masses: a slave in a diamond mine can be very productive, but still remain a slave. Rather, it was because firearms lowered the cost of training a soldier, and thus made the masses valuable as potential soldiers. That gave the masses a bargaining chip which led to better economic and political standing.

If Alice wishes for a world where her labor (e.g. as a programmer) remains economically valuable, but all military jobs go to AI, then humans will lose the "potential soldier bonus" we had for a couple centuries and revert to a powerless, exploited position. The economic importance of our labor won't save us.

Whereas if Bob wishes for a world where all jobs in the economy are done by AI, but somehow humans remain potentially important for war, then humans will be the aristocracy in that world and lead lives of leisure and fun. If I could magically make that future happen, I would.

Of course it's all academic: all military jobs can probably be done by AI even sooner than other jobs. There's already surveillance and drones. But still I wanted to write it up, because so many people today think economic irrelevance is the main issue, when it just isn't.

item.title: Two Ideas for Promoting an AI Security Mindset
item.description:
Here are ideas that are designed to both jolt the AI companies into adopting a security mindset that’s appropriate for handling human-level AIs, and to modestly slow the race to superintelligence. These are not intended as full solutions to either goal.

It is becoming urgent for AI companies to improve the security of their computers, in order to reduce the risk that some arbitrary outsider can take control of the goals of a powerful AI.

1.

I want a bug bounty program loosely patterned after the Hack the Pentagon bug bounty program, with break-ins adjudicated by a government agency.

I propose that bounties be paid to people who can break into an AI company. Have the program plant a canary: a file in the training pipeline that only something with write access to critical systems could modify. Participating hackers get rewards for altering the canary.

The canary reduces the subjectivity of the adjudication, but the agency will still want to make some subjective judgments about the bug severity. I’m thinking of bounties in the $100K to $5M range depending on how hard it looks for the exploit to be used to alter AI weights undetected.

In order to ensure that the AI company faces strong incentives, it should be fined roughly 10 times the rewards that get paid to the hackers.

I want this program to continue indefinitely.

There’s some risk that the program will enable some theft of weights that wouldn’t otherwise be possible. I’m not too concerned about theft of today’s models, but I expect I will become a good deal more concerned about theft of weights in 6 to 12 months.

I suggest that this initially apply to Anthropic and OpenAI, and within a few months be extended to something like 6 or 8 other companies.

2.

My second proposal involves modest changes to liability laws, focused on what happens when a user gives an AI a prompt that causes the AI to do something illegal, or something that would be illegal if a human did it intentionally.

I’m mostly imagining cases where a user asks for something that the AI is unable to accomplish in a legal manner, and for which illegal acts might help the AI accomplish the goal. This should cause significant user pressure on AI companies to reliably report what users should do in order to safely use the AI.

We already have a limited example that outlines the kind of result that I’m hoping for. Microsoft has a Customer Copyright Commitment that says when Microsoft will take responsibility for copyright infringement from using AI, and when it will leave that responsibility to a commercial customer. I’m trying to create an incentive to extend that to all users, and to a much wider set of possible harms.

I want the law to make it clear that at least one of the user or the AI company will be liable for damages, and maybe both. There should be a presumption that users are responsible for determining whether they’re using the AI safely.

Maybe this will be classified as a no-fault loss-allocation rule in cases where all parties claim to have acted reasonably, but I want to at least move in the direction of presuming that many existing AI practices are not as reasonable as people are treating them.

I intend this to create strong pressure for users to switch to AIs whose creators are best able to promise that the AI will behave safely.

This will be especially difficult for agentic tasks where it’s hard to see the connection between the user prompt and the agent’s actions. That’s intentional. Those conditions are where I expect the biggest dangers to come from in the near future. If my proposal ends up functioning as a selective pause on the riskiest capability advances, that seems mostly good.

Open weights are a bit more complex. The creator still needs some liability for the weights that they release. I’m guessing there should also be liability for a person who modifies weights in a way that increases risk. I want to implement the law in a way that preserves the benefits of open weights, but I’m unsure how well those goals can be reconciled. The issue might be moot, because safety concerns are somewhat likely to cause governments to limit the availability of the most powerful open weight models.

I presume this should only apply to AIs above some capability threshold, set somewhere near the level of the current best models. An actual law would need something more precise here – maybe a regulator who certifies models as being below the threshold?

I’m unsure what to do with the case where the user is working for the company that created the AI. The law could hold the individual user personally liable in addition to probable liability for the company. But I’m guessing that even without that provision, the law will provide enough incentive in the near term to accomplish my objectives.

I have some concerns that this law will become less effective when AI companies become reluctant to release their best models to the public. But I’m mainly suggesting this as a near-term stopgap until we can get something better.

Both proposals require some potentially controversial legislation, which could delay implementation more than I’m comfortable with. So the proposals likely depend on the government treating AI risk as unusually urgent.

item.title: The Point of Pressuring the UK Government
item.description:
This is a speech I gave at PauseAI UK's March Against AI Extinction on the 21st of November.

[Crossposted from my blog, BlueprintingHeaven.]

Most of us are not US citizens, but US AI labs threaten every non-US citizen too, so we can't just leave dealing with extinction risk from AI to America.

You can ask the US citizens to talk to their politicians for you, or you can try to talk to US politicians directly, and there are avenues for that, or you can get your government to talk to the American government, which is what PauseAI UK is trying to do.

I want to remind everyone what the point of pressuring the UK government is.

Countries do not exist in isolation from other. Geopolitics exists. If the UK made a costly signal to the US that they genuinely think advanced AI systems could kill every living thing on planet Earth, the policy experts in the US would be terrified. Countries are usually very careful and gentle with their words. A country does not tell another country "this could kill every person on Earth" for no reason. If the British government said that to Washington, serious smart people in DC and American national security will freak out and make things happen. The US government would not ignore the UK government begging for them to stop and saying that they are worried we are all going to die.

Look at the current behaviour of the UK government. The behaviour we see is not that of a government genuinely fighting for its life, for every human life. What would a genuine effort from the UK government to live look like? Ministers would be on the phone to their American counterparts, saying, hey, you are going to kill us, please stop! I implore you to stop! The Foreign Office would be sending serious, strongly worded letters. UK officials would be getting US senators into rooms with AI scientists who can explain why continuing to improve AI capabilities will, by default, lead to human extinction. Every bilateral meeting would have extinction risk from AI as the top priority, ahead of trade and tariffs. Superintelligent AI development would be formally named as a top-tier threat in the National Security Strategy. These are expensive signals that the US knows how to read!

So that is the first thing we are asking for: act now, and act like it is serious.

The UK government should use its G20 presidency to broker a pause treaty between China and the US. The UK government should also not wait until the G20 Leaders' Summit to push on this.

The second thing is about what happens if we get a bilateral pause treaty, a probably fragile one where the US and China are evaluating each others' data centres and constantly on edge. What then? How do we upgrade that treaty and buy more time to solve alignment? Treaties last longer when a trusted third party carries out the evaluations. For nuclear weapons, we have the International Atomic Energy Agency. Nothing like that exists for AI yet. The UK should make that happen. We should lead the way on independent auditors, we should manage the peace, we should keep the pause in place.

If a bilateral treaty is signed, the UK should be ready on day one to help it hold. Right now, the government should fund research into verifying AI chips and training runs. Train inspectors. Work with other countries to set up an independent international body that can check whether a pause is being kept.

These are the things a government would do if they were taking the problem seriously and actually trying to survive.

So, clearly, the government does not understand that their lives are at risk! And that is what PauseAI UK is for.

item.title: Human empowerment in a few fake graphs
item.description:
One view of AI’s trajectory can be captured by this “fake graph” (with the gray region reflecting roughly where we are):


AI is improving in intelligence while human intelligence is fixed. At some point AI will be so powerful that there is no way for humans to comprehend what it is doing, and hence at this point AI will necessarily take over control. The only question is whether the AI will be aligned (i.e. be a “benevolent dictator”) or misaligned (i.e., “if anyone builds it everyone dies”). Indeed, some people in the AI safety community view the former version of a “handover”, “handoff”,  or “passing the torch” to AI as a positive outcome.


I disagree with this view.  I believe that ceding control to AI is by no means necessary, and, even more importantly, we should preserve human autonomy and sovereignty regardless of how aligned we can make AIs.


While the biological capacity of human brains hasn’t changed in the last hundred thousand years, by any reasonable measure the intelligence of humanity as a whole has been growing. Without any biological enhancement, humanity invented concepts like writing, democracy, markets, technology, that enabled us to exercise greater control of our environment. We’ve been creating and hill climbing benchmarks, including the “build cities”,  “feed billions” and “reach the moon” benchmarks, for thousands of years.


Given that, what we really should be comparing is not the intelligence of AI and an average (or even the smartest) human, but rather the intelligence of AI and humanity as a whole, and the latter quantity has been growing over time.


However, humanity’s intelligence has not been growing nearly as fast as AI, and so perhaps all this argument does is buy us some extra time.  That is, the graph looks like this: (with the shaded area still corresponding to the present).


But there is a more optimistic possibility. We have a history of enabling humans to supervise projects of growing complexity. Around the 19th century, science became complex enough so that no one person could know it all (e.g. Thomas Young, who died in 1829 is often called “the last man who knew everything”). In the 20th century, people have constructed artifacts with complexity far outstripping anything that was done before, including aircraft carriers, particle colliders, and large-scale software projects. 


We can use AI itself to expand our mechanisms to comprehend and control AI. That is, we will make sure that humans remain the key decision makers, but use AI to make the space of options legible and controllable by them. This will be “bend the humanity curve upwards” in the graph above.  But, especially with the prospect of AI being used to accelerate its own progress (aka “recursive self improvement”), I believe that if we continue on our current path, AI’s capabilities will grow beyond our ability to comprehend and control it. If that is the case, then using AI to control and explain AI will not be enough to avoid takeover or handoff. Rather we would need to “bend the AI curve downwards” to achieve a graph that looks like the following:


Crucially, we do not necessarily need to “cap” the absolute intelligence of AI, but we may need to cap its rate of progress to maintain human control. I do not have the answers as to how such mechanisms would be implemented, nor to the way to determine the precise “speed limit” for AI growth. But if we want to avoid an AI takeover or handoff, we need to be working on these questions. I suspect we will need a combination of both regulations and technical means to achieve this.


Misalignment and misuse


The discussions above implicitly assumed that AIs are aligned, and that they are not actively trying to destroy the world. But, realistically, some fraction of the total intelligence in the world will be misaligned or misused. So the best case we could hope for is something like:

With the total intelligence (some function of model capabilities and inference compute) directed at aligned goals dominating that directed at misaligned goals. Much of the work of technical AI safety can be thought of as working toward increasing the gap between the two lines above.


Will that be enough? The answer depends on whether you believe in the Vulnerable World Hypothesis. If you believe the VWH, then there is an absolute level of intelligence required to destroy the world, and when misaligned/misused AIs achieve it, this will be “game over”. 

I don’t believe the VWH. I think the technological level that was needed to effectively destroy humanity has increased over time. We are more resilient today than we were in the past. You can’t imagine an army killing possibly up to 10 percent of the world’s population using horses, bows, and swords, as the Mongols did in the 13th century. About half of the European population died from the “Black Death”, which is easily treatable today with antibiotics. This the “world destroying threshold” rises over time, and if we use AI for resilience, we could increase it faster and get a graph that looks like this:


If we combine all of the above, we get a graph that looks like the following:

It requires a combination of using AI to improve resilience and human control, technical AI safety to reduce the powers of misaligned AI, and agreements to ensure AI does not grow too fast for us to maintain these invariants. I believe we can navigate all of these “fake graphs”, and chart a path that ends up in both human prosperity and sovereignty. But we cannot count on this happening by default. Ensuring this path will require a combination of technical means, including progress on safety and alignment, regulations, and international cooperation, including on pacing the rate of AI advancement. We have our work cut out for us!

item.title: Alignment from equivariance III - moraloids and tribal subgroups
item.description:
Reminder (since it's been two years!): we are hoping to build a definition of morality out of pictures like this:

... because such pictures have a very well-studied mathematical structure, enough that we have been able to use the pictures to impose a desirable consistency on computer vision models. In these posts we're hoping this can generalize to imposing moral consistency. This will have various potential advantages: if you can figure out how the pictures should work, there's established ways to build an AI that conforms to it, and it's easy enough to check that someone else's AI conforms to it. And because it's math, this checking may not even be that expensive - you can do loads of trolley problems with one question, so to speak (building the right bunch of diagrams in the first place, now that might be expensive).

Background math: groups, subgroups, and monoids

I'm at risk of losing some of you by being overtly mathematical, but honestly, this bit shouldn't be that hard. If you don't get it, it's because I've explained it badly - over a drink I could have you get it in a minute or two.

Ok, so one of the main kinds of object that mathematicians and physicists have studied for the last 200 years has been "groups". I'll illustrate with two great examples of groups that you'll be familiar with: whole numbers and 3D rotations.

With whole numbers, you can add whole numbers (multiplication isn't necessary to see them as a group). And there's a special number, 0, such that X + 0 = X.

You know 3D rotations as well - you can turn your hand left and right 30° or 90°, turn it up and down and side to side, etc. For any two rotations you can do one, and then the other, and that gets you a third rotation. There's a special, very boring, rotation which is the rotation by zero degrees, call that rotation "I". If R is another rotation, we have that "R then I" = R. So the zero degree rotation does for rotations what the number 0 does for numbers.

There are a huge amount more groups. "Massless universes with a cosmological constant", for example, turned out to be things you can characterize with just groups. To be a group you just need some actions, and a way to combine the actions, and a "neutral" action (like 0 or "I") combining with it changes nothing. You also need "associativity", which we won't worry about today.

For any of the things, there is supposed to be another thing where combining "un-does" what it did. There are ways of changing one moral situations to another that add or throw away information. That means you can't "undo" all changes to moral questions. That is ok - it means that instead of a "group", we have a "monoid", also studied in mathematics.

When mathematicians and physicists study a group, it's often not feasible to list every element - some of them are just too big, and you have to characterize them by describing a recipe of some sort. Famous examples include the Monster Group in pure maths, with approximately 10⁵³ elements (more than you could store on all the world's hardrives), and the U(1) gauge group in physics, which has an infinite dimensional space of elements. Writing down elements of a group, at the end of the day, often means putting numbers in a matrix (or multivectors ✊).

Another useful term is "subgroup". A subgroup means a closed group within a larger group. For example, "multiples of 2" are a subgroup of counting numbers, and "rotations left and right" are a subgroup of 3D rotations. Yes, this will be important :)

Moral strictness and agreement as subgroups

Most of us have moral beliefs that we can use to label some acts as good or bad. Let's say I describe to you a story of Carol doing something, and you find it acceptable. I then slightly "transform" the story, meaning changing bits of it - for example, she needed medicine for her kid, or whatever. The full set of ways I can transform the story without you switching from acceptable to unacceptable - that is your moral monoid (mine might be different). You think of your tribe as giving you beliefs, but I'd say it gives you a monoid, a set of allowed transformations - "I saw X, so I know I can do Y".

Note that more-complicated-to-describe groups and monoids tend to be smaller than simple-to-describe ones (in the sense of what turns out to be a subgroup of what).

Let's say Alice has three moral beliefs and Bob has four, and Bob has all of Alice's beliefs; Bob is therefore stricter than Alice, and fewer things will be acceptable to him. To put it another way, if you start with a proposition that is morally acceptable to Alice and Bob, and then start transforming the proposition in various ways, Bob will reject some modifications that Alice accepts - his group of allowed changes is smaller than Alice's.

Claude points out to me that, coarsely at least, Rawls "veil of ignorance" can be thought of in a group theoretic way: moral actions are those which are still moral if you swap names around. And Kant's categorial imperative is swapping a "Alice does this" with "everyone does this[1].

I think this matters a lot because it is truly a fool's errand to hope we'll solve all of morality. We just want a bit more confident we won't be turned into paperclips! To put it another way: you have your hopes about the future, and your least favorite politician has theirs.

But none of you want us all turned into paperclips!

I take that to mean: we are seeking a monoid of which the moral monoids of all humans are submonoids - our "common ground", which just avoids variations on us being turned into paperclips. We just need a bunch of matrices representing that monoid.

Are we sure the anti-paperclip moraloid exists?

People's moral beliefs are riddled with inconsistencies, and I realized it seems the most autistic thing in the world to build some mathematical structure out of them. For example, Kahneman and Tversky found that silly rewordings of moral propositions change people's stated beliefs - that's the kind of thing to be sensetive to.

But you know, people aren't that bad; the badness just draws our eye a lot. There's a bit of selection bias in the things we choose to talk about (Mercier and Sperber) - those things make us seem more different from each other than we actually are, because why would you spend time talking about all of the things everyone agrees on? It seems likely that lots of our moral intuitions evolved - there was probably some decent selection pressure there, even if it wasn't taking into account future technologies.

Besides: Claude just proved the goddamn Riemann hypothesis. Who on earth are you to say what is feasible with its mathematical abilities?

  1. ^

    for geeks: Rawls has a permutation group, Kant has a trivial monoid



Discuss
